subject: Maths
chapter: Chapter 1: A Square and A Cube
central_question: How can factors, patterns, prime factorisation and inverse operations help us recognise, construct and work with square and cube numbers?
in_scope_units: The 100-locker puzzle and the connection between an odd number of factors and perfect squares.
Square numbers, perfect squares, visual square arrays and patterns in unit digits and trailing zeroes.
Square roots as the inverse of squaring, including estimation and prime-factorisation methods.
Problems on the nearest perfect square, making a number a perfect square and numbers between consecutive squares.
Cubic numbers, unit-cube models and patterns in perfect cubes.
Cube roots and the prime-factorisation method using groups of three equal prime factors.
Historical notes on varga, ghana and mula in Indian mathematics.
The end puzzle on arranging numbers so adjacent pairs add to square numbers.
banned_topics: General laws of exponents beyond what is needed for squares and cubes.
Mensuration formulas for arbitrary solids other than the square and cube models used in the chapter.

known_pitfalls.claim: Every number has an even number of factors.
known_pitfalls.correction: Perfect squares have an odd number of factors because the square root is paired with itself; most non-squares have factors in distinct pairs.

known_pitfalls.claim: A perfect square can end in any digit.
known_pitfalls.correction: A perfect square can end only in 0, 1, 4, 5, 6 or 9.

known_pitfalls.claim: The positive symbol √n gives both square roots of n.
known_pitfalls.correction: √n denotes the positive square root; a positive perfect square has two integral square roots, one positive and one negative.

known_pitfalls.claim: A number is a perfect cube whenever every prime exponent is even.
known_pitfalls.correction: For a perfect cube, every prime exponent must be a multiple of 3, so the prime factors can be grouped into equal triples.

known_pitfalls.claim: A cube may end with exactly two zeroes.
known_pitfalls.correction: The number of trailing zeroes in a perfect cube must be a multiple of 3, so a cube cannot end with exactly two zeroes.

recommended_example_progression: Use the opening 100-locker activity to show why lockers numbered by perfect squares remain open.
